stories.title: Migrating the GitHub Copilot runtime to Rust, using Copilot
stories.snippet: A rewrite this size wasn't affordable before agents. Here's what porting the Copilot agent runtime to 800,000 lines of production Rust actually took. The post Migrating the GitHub Copilot runtime to Rust, using Copilot appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
stories.summary: GitHub rewrote its Copilot agent runtime from TypeScript on Node.js/V8 into more than 800,000 lines of production Rust, with AI agents writing most of the code across 128 incrementally shipped pull requests. The rewrite, completed primarily by a single developer in a few months rather than the year or two a whole team would have needed before agents, addressed performance problems with embedding the JavaScript-based runtime across the Copilot SDK's C#, TypeScript, Python, Rust, Go, and Java clients, each of which previously had to ship Node.js/V8. The new runtime exposes a C ABI for in-process consumption by all six SDK languages while still supporting stdin/stdout or socket-based out-of-process use. It backs numerous Microsoft and GitHub products, including VS Code, Visual Studio, the Copilot CLI, Copilot Studio, and Office applications. The porting effort processed roughly 430,000 lines of TypeScript while the runtime continued to gain capabilities.

stories.title: Size-Specialized Memory Allocation
stories.snippet: Go 1.27 improves performance of small allocations using size-specialized allocation functions.
stories.summary: Go 1.27 introduces faster memory allocation for allocations under 80 bytes, making them 20-30% faster and allocation-heavy programs up to 1% faster. The runtime generates specialized mallocgc variants for each "span class," which encodes both the size class (1-8 bytes through 65-80 bytes) and whether the allocation contains pointers. These specialized functions fall back to generic routines for corner cases like active GC, and the compiler can directly call them when the size is known at compile time, otherwise mallocgc dispatches dynamically. The biggest optimization is memory zeroing, where the compiler can inline clearing instructions when the size is constant, while additional gains come from eliminating span class calculation and manual inlining of helper functions. Stopping at 80 bytes balanced performance gains against instruction cache pressure and binary size. The most common allocation sizes (16 and 24 bytes) benefit most, since these cover interfaces, strings, and slices.

stories.title: Jev means structured output is interesting again
stories.summary: Jev is an AI model that takes human-language prompts but produces only structured output rather than autoregressively generating human-language tokens. Because it produces answers in parallel within a single forward pass, Jev is consistently fast, with response times ranging from about 70ms to 500ms, enabling new low-latency applications such as playing Doom in real time. However, the author argues that fast structured output is already achievable with existing LLMs by pre-filling responses and constraining generation to a single token, suggesting Jev lacks a substantial technical moat. Fine-tuning specifically for structured output may still give Jev an edge, but the model is unlikely to match the reasoning ability of frontier LLMs since it cannot use test-time compute. The author hopes Jev succeeds and inspires competition in the fast-structured-output space.

stories.title: Automated Instruction Encoding Synthesis for Modern GPU ISA Compression
stories.snippet: Modern GPU kernels increasingly stress the instruction supply path, while fixed instruction containers can leave substantial footprint slack. This paper presents an automated encoding-synthesis framework that treats instruction layout as a constrained slot-assignment problem over a validated instruction-form field specification. The formulation separates semantic field identity from physical bit positions and supports tied, pinned, and free placement constraints, making it applicable when recurring decoded fields are not frozen by a public format contract. stories.summary: The paper presents an automated encoding-synthesis framework that treats GPU instruction layout as a constrained slot-assignment problem, separating semantic field identity from physical bit positions and supporting tied, pinned, and free placement constraints. The framework is instantiated for NVIDIA SASS by normalizing raw public encoding text into a machine-readable specification and validating a resulting disassembler against nvdisasm on 3.78 million instructions, which is released as an open benchmark. Using CP-SAT synthesis, the approach generates both fixed-length and variable-length encodings, achieving a 33% instruction-footprint reduction on 142 Blackwell kernel inputs through variable-length synthesis, with comparable gains on Ampere and Hopper. Against a decoder generated from the NVIDIA-observed 128-bit layout, fixed-length synthesis cuts decoder area by 16%. The generated fetch/decode RTL meets 1.5 GHz in TSMC 22 nm with a replicated area delta of 0.12% of a GA100-class die, while the footprint savings correspond to roughly 9× that logic cost in instruction-SRAM bit-cell area.

stories.title: Revisiting Distributed Sign-Based Variance Reduction
stories.snippet: Sign-based methods reduce communication costs in distributed environments, but aggregating local signs can introduce bias when data are heterogeneous. As a result, existing sign-based variance reduction methods fail to obtain the optimal convergence rates. In this paper, we solve this problem and obtain optimal rates for both nonconvex stochastic and finite-sum optimization. We first give a counterexample showing that majority voting can fail to approach stationary points even with exact local gradients. Motivated by this limitation, we propose tracking the global gradient at the server through unbiased compression of recursive gradient increments. stories.summary: Sign-based methods reduce communication costs in distributed machine learning, but aggregating local signs can introduce bias when data are heterogeneous, causing existing sign-based variance reduction methods to miss optimal convergence rates. The authors present a counterexample showing that majority voting can fail to approach stationary points even with exact local gradients. To overcome this limitation, they propose tracking the global gradient at the server through unbiased compression of recursive gradient increments. This approach yields convergence rates of O(√(d/K) + √d(a/(nK))^(1/3)) for the ℓ1-norm and O(√(a/K) + √a/(nK)^(1/3)) for the ℓ2-norm, where K is the iteration number, n is the number of workers, d is the dimension, and a=1+ω with ω denoting the compressor's relative variance. For finite-sum problems with M components, the method combines periodic exact gradient refreshes with compressed component-gradient differences, achieving sample complexities that match corresponding centralized bounds.

stories.summary: The paper, authored by Yu-Ting Lee, Samuel Yen-Chi Chen, and Huan-Hsin Tseng, introduces QFWP-ANO, a novel architecture designed to enhance quantum neural networks (QNNs). Traditional variational quantum circuits (VQCs) are limited by local measurements, and while adaptive non-local observables (ANO) help by jointly optimizing circuit parameters and multi-qubit measurements, existing ANO-based VQCs use a single static observable that remains unchanged across all inputs. To address this limitation, QFWP-ANO employs a classical hypernetwork to dynamically program VQC parameters and/or non-local observables conditioned on each specific input. On multivariate time-series forecasting across four ETT datasets, the proposed method achieves the lowest mean squared error in 16 of 20 settings and the second-lowest in the remaining four, outperforming ANO-based and other strong baselines. Additionally, QFWP-ANO consistently surpasses ANO-VQCs on reinforcement learning tasks. These results establish input-conditioned ANO as an effective approach for improving QNNs.

stories.title: Fallacy Benchmarks Measure Scheme Recognition, Not Fallacy Detection
stories.snippet: Fallacy-detection benchmarks pair fallacy classes with a single "valid" or "none" class that takes everything data collection did not label as a fallacy. This construction is misleading: a classifier can learn cues that do well on this class without learning to tell a fallacy from a correct argument. We show that the low false-positive rates benchmarks report are an artifact of how the class is built, not evidence of detection ability. The most informative negative for a fallacy is a correct argument using the same argumentation scheme, and such arguments are at most a few percent of the valid class across the four benchmarks we examined. Evaluated on constructed scheme-matched negatives, false-positive rates rise from 16.6% to 58.9% on CoCoLoFa and from 5.7% to 62.0% on Reddit. That rate
stories.summary: Existing fallacy-detection benchmarks pair each fallacy class with a single "valid" or "none" class containing everything not labeled as a fallacy, a construction the authors argue is misleading. Because correct arguments using the same argumentation scheme represent only a few percent of these valid classes, classifiers can achieve low false-positive rates by learning scheme recognition rather than the ability to distinguish fallacious from correct arguments. When evaluated on scheme-matched correct negatives, false-positive rates rise dramatically, from 16.6% to 58.9% on CoCoLoFa and from 5.7% to 62.0% on Reddit. In a controlled comparison, classifiers label scheme-matched correct arguments as the source fallacy type 40.9 points more often than wrong-scheme arguments, while wrong-scheme items are identified by their actual scheme 85.9% of the time versus 0.4% for the source type. The same dissociation appears in three zero-shot LLM detectors that never saw these benchmarks. The authors release their constructed items as Scheme Foils and argue that reported false-positive rates should not be trusted until the valid class is audited for scheme-matched coverage.

stories.title: CoRe-MARL: Cooperative Redistribution Under Unknown Dynamics Using Recurrent Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
stories.snippet: Emergency management assistance programs, such as relief distribution, are essential for delivering necessary supplies to affected communities. However, these programs operate in a decentralized network of local centers that face uncertain local demand and supply dynamics, resulting in inconsistent avail- ability of local services. Redistribution of supplies among these local centers reduces these imbalances, but the centers often make decisions independently, with limited information and disrupted transportation. This study develops CoRe-MARL, a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework, by formulating a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process (Dec-POMDP). We treat each center as an agent that learns a redistribution policy to improve the service i
stories.summary: The authors introduce CoRe-MARL, a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning framework designed to optimize supply redistribution among decentralized local centers in emergency relief distribution networks operating under uncertain demand and supply dynamics. The problem is formulated as a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process, where each center acts as an agent learning a redistribution policy aimed at improving service in the worst-served region, reducing service gaps across regions, and protecting network-wide service. The approach incorporates a recurrent network to capture evolving supply and demand dynamics without direct observation, paired with multi-agent proximal policy optimization for centralized training and decentralized execution. In simulated environments with diverse trajectories, the recurrent MAPPO was compared against recurrent independent PPO and a local-only heuristic, demonstrating reduced service gaps and enhanced service for the worst-served center while maintaining competitive network-wide performance. The framework also showed consistent results across varied trajectory patterns, highlighting its adaptability to uncertain and evolving dynamics.

stories.title: Show HN: An e-ink frame that hears birds and draws them as 1800s illustrations
stories.snippet: See also: Avian Visitors - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48343424 - May 2026 (20 comments)
stories.summary: Fugleramme is an open-source project that turns a Raspberry Pi with an Inky Impression e-ink panel into a live-updating bird display, detecting birds by sound via BirdNET-Go and rendering them as hand-curated 1800s natural-history illustrations on textured paper. The creator curated over 800 public-domain cut-outs covering more than 400 species, sorted by body mass and packed onto pages with empty windows showing a bare perch. Currently live in a Bergen, Norway kitchen window, it works best for Nordic, British, and central European species, with broader European and North American coverage planned. The frame can run with or without the e-ink panel as a web kiosk, and ships with multiple install options including a one-line script for Pi, Docker images, and a Python development setup. The project shares no code or art with similar projects like AvianVisitors or featherframe, and code is MIT licensed.

stories.title: Reverse-engineered Jev-like model
stories.summary: The repository offers an independent starter model that mimics Jev's input and output shape: it takes a piece of text and a list of options, then returns one probability per option in a single pass. Each option becomes a query vector that assigns attention weights to context tokens, producing a context vector scored by a shared dot product and normalized with a softmax. The default encoder learns byte embeddings from scratch, though users can optionally attach a frozen Hugging Face encoder like Qwen2.5-0.5B. Training data uses JSONL files with context, options, and a label index. In local experiments, the one-pass scorer reached about 98% accuracy on synthetic menus and roughly 26-29% on target-disjoint Wikispeedia next-click data, depending on the encoder, while running about 100 times faster than a small decoder writing 400 tokens. The release is licensed under MIT and explicitly notes it is a research starter, not a reproduction of Jev or TypeSafe's private training method.

stories.title: Introducing System One Models and Jev
stories.summary: Diogo Almeida, formerly of OpenAI, founded TypeSafe AI and announced the release of Jev, the company's first System One Model, available in early access. Jev is built around Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD) and is designed to make fast, structured decisions that software can consume directly, replacing sequential string generation with parallel sampling of type-safe outputs. The company claims Jev matches the intelligence of frontier LLMs on System One tasks while being roughly two orders of magnitude faster and cheaper, with response times between 70ms and 500ms compared to 3–329 seconds for existing models, and input pricing of $0.042 per million tokens with free outputs. Because possible outputs are defined in advance, Jev cannot make type errors or hallucinate, and every answer includes calibrated probabilities and confidence scores. Target use cases include AI-powered workflows acting as fuzzy decision rules, map-reduce processing over large datasets, real-time applications, and verifying or scoring outputs from other LLMs.

stories.title: An update on Wayback Machine access
stories.summary: Mark Graham, Director of the Wayback Machine, posted an update on September 15, 2026, addressing ongoing access issues with the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine. The service has been overwhelmed by waves of high-volume automated traffic, prompting the team to put protections in place to keep it running. As part of these efforts, they rewrote the message users see when blocked with a 429 "too many requests" error. While these safeguards are necessary, they occasionally block real users by mistake. The team is actively working to improve their ability to distinguish abusive bots from genuine users. Anyone incorrectly blocked is encouraged to email info@archive.org with their operating system, browser, and IP address so the issue can be investigated.

stories.title: Apple Reference Image: A New Approach for Verified Photography
stories.summary: Apple Reference Image is a new opt-in camera mode debuting on iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max that creates securely timestamped reference images accurately reflecting what the device's sensor captured. The system works in two phases: first, a secure digital negative is created when the sensor cryptographically signs pixel data immediately after capture, preventing tampering; then, Private Cloud Compute (PCC) processes this negative into a viewable image within a verifiable, privacy-preserving environment. Apple Reference Image embeds both a lower-bound and upper-bound cryptographic timestamp, provided by Apple's timestamp service on roughly 15-minute intervals, guaranteeing the photo was taken between the two times. The system is designed to resist sensor tampering, cryptographic attacks, and software jailbreaks, with fraudulent images revocable without exposing the photographer's identity. Unlike C2PA-based approaches, which certify edits after capture, Apple Reference Image secures the entire pipeline from raw sensor data to final image, providing stronger semantic authenticity, resilience, and privacy guarantees.

stories.title: Mistral X Mozilla: Private, Multilingual AI Browsing
stories.summary: Mistral and Mozilla have announced a partnership to bring open, private, and multilingual AI to web browsing through Firefox Smart Window (beta), Mozilla's AI browsing assistant. Smart Window helps users understand complex searches, recall previously clicked content, and source information from their browser tabs. Mistral will power Smart Window initially for users in France and North America, with the United Kingdom and Germany expected to follow later in 2026. Both companies are open source advocates, and Mistral's models are fine-tuned on regional languages and dialects to serve local cultural contexts. The partnership emphasizes user privacy, with conversations not saved on Mozilla's servers by default and Mistral agreeing to zero data retention. Together, the companies aim to extend sovereign, privacy-focused AI from enterprise use to consumers worldwide.
